FOR INDEPENDENT PROCESS SERVERS

A flat serve fee can still be a losing job.

A client paying $65 a serve reads fine right up until the third attempt, the bad address that needs skip tracing, and the 20-mile round trip come out of it. This free calculator finds real net profit for one job, then lets you compare two or three clients' fee schedules by what they actually pay per hour — not their headline base fee.

Everything on this page runs in your browser and nothing is ever uploaded. Your job inputs (attempts, rush/skip-trace flags, mileage, time, costs) are saved locally on this device so you don't retype them next time — Reset to defaults clears them, and Copy shareable link puts them in a URL fragment your browser never sends anywhere. Your client comparison rows are a different promise: they are never saved anywhere, and closing or refreshing the tab clears them. There is no account. We count only anonymous local feature events (job-priced, clients-compared, link-copied, reset) so we can tell whether the calculator gets used — no client names, fees, or job figures are recorded, and Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control turn it off automatically.

Fee looks fine on paper — is it actually worth it?

A $65-a-serve offer can still pay under minimum wage once a hard-to-find defendant and a long drive are netted out. Is this process server fee schedule worth it? works through the arithmetic on a real lowball offer next to a solid one. Already running a caseload through ServeManager or a comparable platform? See how this calculator and ServeManager are different tools — one prices a job, the other runs the business. Tallying attempts, mileage, and a client's fee schedule by hand or in a spreadsheet? See what a hand tally or ad hoc spreadsheet tends to miss — the same formula, applied consistently, across every client.

Common questions

Why does a flat per-serve fee not tell me whether a job is worth taking?

Because the flat fee is priced for the ordinary case -- a good address, one or two attempts, a short drive. A defendant who is hard to find adds attempts and time the base fee never covered, a bad address can mean skip tracing before you can even attempt service, and a long drive burns real fuel and vehicle wear whether or not the client's mileage add-on covers all of it. The same headline fee can be a great job or a losing one depending on those four things.

Does this tool tell me whether service was properly effected or how to serve someone who is avoiding service?

No. This calculator only prices your own job economics from numbers you supply. It does not determine whether service was validly effected under any state's rules of civil procedure, whether you are licensed, bonded, or registered to serve process in a given jurisdiction, or whether an affidavit of service will hold up in court -- verify all of that independently.

Why does vehicle cost count for every mile driven, but mileage revenue only for miles beyond what is included?

Because that is what actually happens on the job: fuel and wear cost you money for every mile you drive, but a client's mileage add-on typically only pays once you are past the miles their base fee already covers. Counting only the billed miles as a cost is the most common way a job's real profit gets overstated.

Does anything about my job or client fee schedules get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and the client fee-schedule rows you type into the comparison table are never saved anywhere -- they exist only in the page while it is open. The job inputs above are different: those are saved locally on this device, so you don't retype them, and a shareable link can carry them to another device. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

← Back to the process server fee & route profit calculator

Is this process server fee schedule worth it?

A fee schedule reads as one number — "$65 a serve" or "$40 a serve plus mileage" — and that number is the one thing it does not tell you: how much the job actually pays once you count what it takes to close it. Two real-shaped schedules below, run through the same arithmetic, end up in very different places.

The solid schedule

Base fee $65, covering two attempts and ten miles. This job took three attempts and a 20-mile round trip, no rush, no skip trace, plus the standard $10 affidavit fee — about 54 minutes of drive, on-site, and paperwork time combined.

Amount
Gross revenue$96.70
Vehicle cost$3.60
Fixed job cost$5.00
Net profit$88.10
Effective hourly rate$97.89/hr
Profit margin91.1%

Add-on revenue alone (the extra attempt, mileage, and affidavit fee) already covers this job's cost, so the break-even base fee is negative — this client would still be worth serving for even at a $0 base rate, on this job's numbers.

The lowball schedule

Base fee $25, covering one attempt and five miles — cheaper-looking on the flyer. This defendant took six attempts and needed a skip trace after the first address turned out to be stale, plus an 80-mile round trip on a $0.15/mile add-on that does not come close to the $0.22/mile it actually costs to drive. Two hours of drive time, ninety minutes on-site across six attempts, and eighteen minutes of paperwork.

Amount
Gross revenue$76.25
Vehicle cost$17.60
Fixed job cost$8.00
Net profit$50.65
Effective hourly rate$13.33/hr
Profit margin66.4%

$50.65 and a 66.4% margin look fine in isolation. They are not the number that matters here: this job took 3.8 hours of your day, one attempt short of a full workday's worth of driving and knocking, and paid barely above minimum wage for it. A server who only tracks per-job profit, not per-hour, keeps taking these.

The difference is attempts, address quality, and distance — not the base fee

$40 separated these two base fees, and $84.56/hr separated what they actually paid. The lowball client's low per-attempt and per-mile add-ons meant a hard-to-find defendant and a long drive were the server's problem, not the client's — the flat fee never adjusted for either. Run your own numbers before you accept the next job from a client whose fee schedule you have not checked against a realistic attempt count and drive distance.

Common questions

Why does the lowball schedule still show a profit if it's a bad deal?

Because none of its costs disappeared -- vehicle cost and this job's fixed-cost share apply no matter which client you serve for. Only the attempts, address quality, and distance changed, and together they cut the effective hourly rate from $97.89/hr to $13.33/hr, which the flat base fee alone never shows.

What is the fastest way to tell two client fee schedules apart?

Compare effective hourly rate, not the base fee. The solid schedule pays $97.89/hr on this job; the lowball schedule pays $13.33/hr for a harder version of the same job -- a $40 gap in base fee hides an $84.56/hr gap in what the job actually paid.

vs-doing-it-by-hand.html.text:
← Process Server Fee & Route Profit Calculator

This calculator vs. doing it by hand or a spreadsheet

Base fee, plus extra-attempt, rush, and skip-trace add-ons, plus mileage revenue past what's included, minus your vehicle cost — that's arithmetic anyone can do on a notepad or in a spreadsheet. The part that's easy to get wrong, or to skip entirely, is doing it the same way for every job and turning the result into what the job actually paid per hour, especially once you're tallying a second or third client's fee schedule against the same numbers.

What each approach actually does

By hand or in a spreadsheet, you can add up a serve's revenue — base fee, extra attempts beyond what's included, a rush or skip-trace surcharge, and mileage past the included distance — and subtract your vehicle cost and the affidavit and fixed-cost share. All of that is straightforward addition and subtraction, and a correctly built spreadsheet gets it exactly right. What it does not give you, unless you build it in yourself, is a place that keeps the client's mileage rate and your own vehicle cost per mile as two clearly separate numbers — it is easy to tally only the billed miles as a cost and overstate profit — or a built-in step that turns a dollar figure into an effective hourly rate, which most hand tallies skip until after a run of bad jobs makes the gap obvious.

This calculator runs the identical formula every time: extra attempts beyond what's included, rush and skip-trace add-ons, mileage revenue only for miles past the included distance, vehicle cost for every mile actually driven, and net profit divided by total time (drive, on-site, and paperwork) to show effective hourly rate and the break-even base fee. The built-in client comparison table then applies that same formula consistently across two, three, or four clients' fee schedules side by side, so the ranking reflects what each client actually pays per hour for the same job — not which tally happened to be built more carefully that day.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What does one serve at one client's fee schedule actually net?Either — a correctly built spreadsheet gets this exactly right too.
What's the effective hourly rate, not just the profit in dollars?This calculator shows it every time. By hand, it's a division step most tallies leave out.
Which of two or three clients' fee schedules actually pays best for the same job?This calculator's client comparison table — the same formula, applied consistently to every row.
Is the client's mileage rate the same thing as my own vehicle cost per mile?No — a hand tally sometimes conflates them. This calculator keeps them as two separate fields.
My situation has a wrinkle this calculator doesn't model (a stepped per diem, a shared vehicle, a tiered attempt fee).A spreadsheet you build yourself — it can represent any rule you can describe.
Is anything I type uploaded anywhere?No, either way — a local spreadsheet and this calculator both keep your numbers on your own device.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Can't I just tally a serve's profit by hand or in a spreadsheet?

Yes — base fee, plus extra-attempt, rush, and skip-trace add-ons, plus mileage revenue past what's included, minus your vehicle cost and the affidavit and fixed-cost share, is straightforward addition and subtraction. A correctly built spreadsheet gets that part exactly right. Where a hand tally or a quick spreadsheet formula stops short is turning that dollar figure into an effective hourly rate, and doing the same arithmetic the same way for a second and third client's fee schedule without dropping a line — that's the part this calculator exists for.

What does a spreadsheet not catch that this calculator does?

Two things a blank spreadsheet has no built-in reminder for. First, a client's mileage rate and your own vehicle cost per mile are two different numbers — one is what the client pays you past the included miles, the other is what fuel and wear actually cost you for every mile driven — and it is easy to tally only the billed miles as a cost, which overstates profit. Second, a dollar profit on its own does not say whether the job paid well: this calculator always divides net profit by total time (drive, on-site, and paperwork) to show effective hourly rate, which a hand tally usually skips because it takes an extra step most people don't bother adding until after a bad month.

Why is comparing several clients' fee schedules harder than it looks?

Because it means building the same formula correctly two or three times, under time pressure, and applying every add-on and cost the identical way for each client. A dropped extra-attempt fee for one client or a skipped skip-trace charge for another changes which client looks like the better one to keep serving for, without showing an error anywhere. This calculator's client comparison table runs the exact same formula for every row, so the ranking reflects what each client actually pays per hour for the same job, not which tally happened to be built more carefully.

Is this calculator affiliated with any spreadsheet or notebook app?

There is nothing to be affiliated with. This page compares against doing the arithmetic by hand or building your own spreadsheet — a generic method, not any specific company or product — so it names no spreadsheet application, notebook app, or vendor at all.

vs-servemanager.html.text:
← Process Server Fee & Route Profit Calculator

This calculator vs. ServeManager

Two different shapes: ServeManager is an account-based platform for running a process serving company's whole caseload, including tracking attempts, generating the affidavit, and invoicing the client once a job is done. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what does this specific serve actually net, once extra attempts, rush or skip-trace add-ons, mileage, and your own vehicle cost and time come out of the base fee — and which client's fee schedule really pays the best hourly rate.

What each tool is for

ServeManager is case management software used by process serving companies and agencies to run a caseload: tracking jobs and individual service attempts, generating the affidavit of service once a job is complete, and invoicing clients, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. ServeManager's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that kind of case management software describe logging an attempt, producing a court-ready affidavit, and billing the client once a job is closed; none describe working out whether a flat per-serve fee still clears the server's own vehicle cost and time once a third attempt and a bad address needing skip tracing are netted out — which is what this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what ServeManager does. It does not track a caseload, log individual service attempts, generate an affidavit, or invoice a client. It takes a base fee, the attempts included versus the attempts it actually took, a rush or skip-trace add-on, mileage revenue against the server's own vehicle cost per mile, drive and paperwork time, and a per-job share of fixed costs, and turns that into net profit and an effective hourly rate for one job — plus a side-by-side ranking of several clients' fee schedules by what they actually pay per hour for the same job, not just their headline base fee. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I need to track a caseload, log service attempts, generate affidavits, and invoice clients across an ongoing business.ServeManager, or a comparable case management platform — running that ongoing operation is not something this calculator does.

Which client's fee schedule actually pays the best hourly rate for the same job, not just the highest headline fee?This calculator's client comparison table.
Is a flat per-serve rate still worth taking once a hard-to-find defendant and a long drive are netted out?This calculator's own worked fee-schedule example.
I need to log this job's attempts, generate the affidavit, and bill the client once it's closed.ServeManager — built as an account-based platform for exactly that job.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. ServeManager's tools are used through a paid account.

Most independent process servers get different value from each: ServeManager (or a comparable case management platform) for tracking a caseload, generating affidavits and invoicing clients across an ongoing business as an account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what one job actually nets and which client's fee schedule really pays best before deciding whether to take the next assignment. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a logged attempt, an affidavit, or an invoice.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or ServeManager?

They do different jobs, and a process server of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. ServeManager is case management software used by process serving companies and agencies to track jobs and service attempts, generate affidavits of service, and invoice clients, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. This calculator does one narrower thing: it takes a base fee, extra-attempt and rush/skip-trace add-ons, mileage revenue against the server's own vehicle cost, and drive and paperwork time, and turns that into net profit and an effective hourly rate for one job -- then ranks several clients' fee schedules by what they actually pay per hour for the same job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A server already tracking a caseload, generating affidavits, and invoicing clients across an ongoing business is better served by ServeManager or a comparable case management platform; a server who wants an instant, private answer to what one job actually nets -- and which client's fee schedule really pays the best hourly rate -- is in the right place here.

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by ServeManager. ServeManager is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.
